name: Balanced static scorer
description: Scores how well a project divides its work into solutions and parts as one balanced number: seven dimensions read from the code and records without a model, each a share inside a budget (graded by how far over it a part goes for size, with imports of the project's shared kernel told apart from reach-ins), folded by a geometric mean within a dimension and a fixed weighted mean across them; stage two adds co-change mined from git history to the coupling dimension.
advantages: Free and takes seconds on a large repository; names the worst offenders of each dimension; no single dimension can win; reads any Python project, using records and tests where they exist.
disadvantages: Judges structure by what code shows, so a well-named split that is wrong for the domain scores the same as a right one; budgets are defaults a project tunes.

name: File size only
description: Scores how well a project divides its work into solutions and parts as one number from the size dimension alone: functions, modules, folders and depth inside their budgets, with nothing about coupling, copies, scope or behavior.
advantages: The simplest scorer and the one most linters already offer; a bound that shows what the balanced number adds.
disadvantages: Shrinking files and functions wins it, so it prefers the project cut into tiny files and cannot see an arm off its interface, a library that names its consumer, copied arithmetic or a missing contract.

name: Expert scoping review
description: Scores how well a project divides its work into solutions and parts as one number from an expert model's judgement: it reads an outline of the project (units, files, sizes, imports) and scores each dimension with offenders in the same report shape; it needs a provider, costs a call per project and is run only with Joshua's approval.
advantages: Can judge what static code cannot: whether the split fits the domain, and whether two solutions are really one job.
disadvantages: Costs money, varies between runs and models, and an expert that reads only an outline can be wrong about what the code does.
